Other IDs in the proposed group (mu_2024_1_D016, D020, D040, D042) describe different aspects (e.g., revenue, specific product launches) or are unrelated to the core SBU definition scope provided by D039, so they are excluded to ensure topic specificity. mu_2023_1_D027 and D030 are kept together as they jointly describe the SBU scope and products in 2023.

comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's four reportable segments are Data Center, Client, Gaming, and Embedded, each encompassing specific product lines for data centers, client devices, gaming hardware, and embedded solutions.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and AMD define their business structure by end-market segments (data center, client/PC, consumer), but they differ in organizational scope and specific product offerings within those markets. MU's Storage Business Unit (SBU) is a distinct operational unit focused solely on SSDs and NAND components across data center, PC, and consumer segments. In contrast, AMD organizes its entire company into four reportable segments (Data Center, Client, Gaming, Embedded), where 'Client' and 'Data Center' overlap with MU's markets but include CPUs and GPUs rather than storage. Specifically, MU identifies 'client SSDs' as part of the PC market (mu_2024_1_P041_S002), while AMD defines its Client segment as including 'CPUs, APUs, and chipsets for desktops and notebooks' (amd_2024_1_P013_S003). Similarly, while MU's data center market includes 'enterprise and cloud SSDs' (mu_2024_1_P041_S002), AMD's Data Center segment focuses on 'AI accelerators, server CPUs, GPUs... for data centers' (amd_2024_1_P013_S002).

comparisons.peer_summary: The company supplies optical components for Ethernet networking, storage, and telecommunication markets to enable high-speed data transmission through optical fibers.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and AVGO disclose involvement in the storage market, but their roles and products differ significantly. MU is a manufacturer of end-user storage solutions (SSDs) and NAND components sold directly into data center, PC, and consumer markets. AVGO, conversely, supplies optical components that 'enable the high speed reception and transmission of data' for the storage market, acting as an enabler for networking infrastructure rather than a primary storage device manufacturer. MU's text states: 'SBU includes SSDs and component-level storage solutions sold into the data center, PC, and consumer markets' (mu_2024_1_P041_S001). AVGO's text states: 'We supply a wide array of optical components to the Ethernet networking, storage... markets' (avgo_2024_1_P008_S007). While both touch the 'storage' topic, MU provides the storage medium itself, whereas AVGO provides the connectivity components for data transmission within storage and network infrastructures.

• Fiber Optic Components: We supply a wide array of optical components to the Ethernet networking, storage, and access, metro- and long-haul telecommunication markets. Our optical components enable the high speed reception and transmission of data through optical fibers.

comparisons.peer_summary: Due to high capital requirements, Intel is expanding its foundry business for external customers, offering wafer fabrication, packaging, chiplets, and software/services, differentiated by leading-edge technology, committed US/EU capacity, and an IP portfolio including x86 cores.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and INTC discuss semiconductor manufacturing strategies and capacity, but from different business models. MU's SBU relies on internal or contracted NAND manufacturing to produce storage components. INTC explicitly describes its IDM 2.0 strategy to expand its 'foundry business for external customers' due to high capital requirements, offering 'wafer fabrication, packaging, chiplets, and software/services'. While MU's disclosure focuses on the *products* sold (SSDs/NAND) into markets, INTC's disclosure focuses on the *manufacturing service* model. INTC states: 'We are seeking to build a world-class foundry business also serving external customers... Our foundry offerings include four components: wafer fabrication, packaging, chiplets, and software and services' (intc_2024_1_P014_S003, intc_2024_1_P014_S004). MU's text describes the *result* of its manufacturing/supply chain: 'SBU includes SSDs and component-level storage solutions' (mu_2024_1_P041_S001). The core similarity is the semiconductor focus; the difference is MU's product-centric view vs. INTC's foundry-service-centric view.

comparisons.peer_summary: Leading cloud service providers and consumer internet companies utilize NVIDIA's data-center-scale accelerated computing platforms to enable and enrich services for billions of end users, including AI assistants and search.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and NVDA identify 'data center' and 'cloud' services as key end-markets for their products. MU's Storage Business Unit sells 'enterprise and cloud SSDs' to the data center market. NVDA's Data Center segment sells 'accelerated computing platforms' to 'leading cloud service providers'. MU states: 'The data center market includes enterprise and cloud SSDs... while the PC market consists of client SSDs' (mu_2024_1_P041_S002). NVDA states: 'The world's leading cloud service providers... use our data center-scale accelerated computing platforms' (nvda_2024_1_P007_S001). The similarity lies in targeting the same broad infrastructure sector (data centers/cloud), but the products are distinct: MU provides storage components, while NVDA provides computing accelerators. Both are critical infrastructure components for these markets.

sentences.text: The data center market includes enterprise and cloud SSDs and enterprise NAND components while the PC market consists of client SSDs.

The world's leading cloud service providers, or CSPs, and consumer internet companies use our data center-scale accelerated computing platforms to enable, accelerate or enrich the services they deliver to billions of end users, including AI solutions and assistants, search, recommendations, social networking, online shopping, live video, and translation.

comparisons.comparison: Both MU and QCOM disclose market outlooks for the 'PC' or 'handset' consumer markets, but focus on different device categories and growth metrics. MU's SBU includes 'client SSDs' for the 'PC market'. QCOM focuses on 'handset volumes' (smartphones) with estimated growth rates. MU defines its market segment: 'the PC market consists of client SSDs' (mu_2024_1_P041_S002). QCOM provides a specific volume forecast: 'For calendar year 2024, we estimate that consumer demand for 3G, 4G, and 5G handset volumes will increase by a low-to-mid-single digit percentage' (qcom_2024_1_P011_S002). Both address consumer electronics end-markets, but MU identifies the specific storage product type within the PC segment, whereas QCOM provides the aggregate volume growth trend for mobile handsets.
